item.title: How to Start a Side Project While Working Full-Time
item.dc:creator: Margaret Cole
item.description: What I’ve learned building VIRI around a 9-to-5.
item.content:encoded:
Two months ago, the idea came to me while I was out grabbing coffee with a close friend: “I’ve got it, a social media platform that connects you to people in your workout classes.”

Graduating college and moving to a new city is a period of life filled with extreme change and many unanswered questions. Will I like my job? What if my apartment has problems? How do I choose the right health insurance plan? Why is everything so expensive? And on top of all that, how do I actually make long-lasting adult friendships?

This last question was one that I grappled with internally for months. Thankfully, I found a group very early on, and we hung out every week. That was, until I actually settled into the demands of my job and had to balance marathon training on top of it. While I was with my friends, my mind constantly wandered to thoughts like, What time do I have to leave to get home early enough to wake up and run? I had so many competing priorities that it was impossible to be present, even when I was physically in the same room as them. And so I slowly started drifting away from the group to prioritize my training.

There was, however, one way of hanging out with friends that worked with my schedule: going to workout classes together. Long story short, this worked for about a month, until our ClassPass trials ran out of classes that fit both of our schedules.

So I was back to square one. A few days later, the idea hit me. Even in the 5 a.m. and 6 a.m. classes I took, the room was always full, usually with women who looked to be about my age and who clearly had the motivation to get up early and work out, just like I did. The people were there; I just didn’t know how to reach them. Hence the social media platform, because in today’s age, that’s how we connect.

I knew my idea had potential; I just had to act on it. The only minor problems were that I had no idea how to build a website, and I had to work around my 9-to-5. Which brings me to step one.

1. Find your hours

I knew that if I was actually going to make my idea a reality, I had to dedicate a lot of time to it. It couldn’t just be something I worked on passively when I felt like it. It had to be a priority that I intentionally built into my schedule. So before anything else, I blocked the time on my calendar and held myself accountable to it: 60 hours a month, or roughly 2 hours a day. It might sound like a lot, but for any venture to really take shape, I think this is the bare minimum.

I didn’t just set a monthly goal; I also built a tracker that I’d go into every day to log how much time I’d spent on VIRI. If my hours were lagging at the end of a given week, I knew that something needed to change, or that I had to spend more time on it the next day.

2. Start small: pick one goal for the first month

Starting a side project can be very overwhelming at first. It seems like there are a million things to do, and they’re all pulling you in different directions. I experienced this quite often in the early stages of building VIRI. I could build the website, figure out the revenue plan, grow VIRI’s social media presence, write articles; the tasks were endless. Some days I would look back on three hours of work and realize I hadn’t made any actual progress, because I didn’t have a clear sense of direction.

I realized that if I wanted to make real progress, I had to pick one specific goal to work toward in the first month, which for me was launching the website. With a clear sense of direction, I was infinitely more productive with my time. Each day when I sat down to work on VIRI, I knew exactly what still needed to be done.

3. Use tools that save time

When I came up with the idea for VIRI, I didn’t know the first thing about building a website. I literally had no clue where to even start. I knew my boyfriend had built a simple website before, so I told him my idea and asked what the easiest way to build VIRI would be. I shouldn’t have been surprised, but the answer was AI tools. And so Claude quickly became my best friend.

Starting an independent venture takes an incredible amount of time, so finding tools that help you build more efficiently is crucial to your success.

4. Protect your energy

This has been absolutely key to my progress with VIRI. I could choose to work on VIRI for hours into the night, or swap out less important priorities for a little extra work, but setting boundaries is essential to long-term success. Without limits, you burn out, and then both the project and your job suffer. So I have intentionally held on to my healthy habits while building VIRI, which means that when the clock hits 8 p.m., I close my computer, and I never swap a workout for VIRI work. Because I’ve kept my other priorities and a healthy balance, I have never dreaded VIRI. It’s still something I’m excited to work on every morning.

Even when progress is slow, I still choose to build, to write, and to post. VIRI allows me to keep learning and growing, which, at the end of the day, is all you can really ask of a side project. So here are a few things to remember as you start your own:

  • Progress isn’t just measured in numbers. The skills you build, the confidence you gain and having something that’s yours count too.
  • It changes how your workday feels. A side project can make a 9-to-5 feel less like your whole identity.
  • Small steps add up. Sometimes you have to step back to realize how much progress you’ve made.

So if there’s an idea sitting in your notes app right now, consider this your sign to block off the hours and start. Your first month doesn’t have to be perfect. It just has to happen.
